segs.label: HOOK (drop on "drops")
segs.text: You're strapped to a sled above the deepest trench on Earth, and in five seconds it drops.

segs.label: HOOK / teasers x4
segs.text: It won't stop for eleven kilometres, and on the way down you'll meet a squid with an eye wider than your face, a whale that holds one breath longer than your whole trip, the last fish on the planet, and, almost at the bottom, something that should never have made it there.

segs.label: MASTER QUESTION (= title)
segs.text: So how many times does the ocean kill you before you reach the bottom? Let's count.

segs.label: RUNG 1 (0-1 km) entry + rule 1
segs.text: Ten metres down, your ears already hurt, because the pressure on you has doubled. Pinch your nose, blow, pop. And yes, you can breathe down here. That's rule one, so don't ask how.

segs.label: Rule 2 + FORMAT REVEAL (ALIVE meter, CHEATS LEFT 3)
segs.text: Rule two: every time the ocean kills you, you get a cheat that brings you back, but you only get three, and when they're gone, so are you. That's what this meter is for. Are you still alive? Right now, yes.

segs.label: Rule 3 (planted for the twist) + sink rate
segs.text: Rule three: no submarine. Fewer people have ever reached the bottom than have been to space, all of them inside one, so you'll be the first thing of ours to get there without. At this slow walking pace, the trip takes about three hours.

segs.label: RUNG 1 colour loss, TWILIGHT named
segs.text: Then the colours go, red first, then orange, then yellow, until everything is blue. Welcome to the twilight zone.

segs.label: RUNG 1 record (701 m)
segs.text: At seven hundred metres, you pass a quiet record. A diver in a French test chamber was once squeezed to exactly this pressure, and no human has felt more.

segs.label: RUNG 1 creature: sperm whale
segs.text: Then you feel a clicking so loud it buzzes in your chest. A sperm whale is hunting somewhere in the dark, and its clicks are the loudest sound any animal makes.

segs.label: RUNG 1 plant ("its dinner")
segs.text: Relax, it's after squid, not you. Keep that in mind, because you're about to meet its dinner.

segs.label: RUNG 1 threshold 1 km, MIDNIGHT named
segs.text: One kilometre, and you've reached the midnight zone, where the sunlight is gone for good, and from here down, the only light is alive.

segs.label: RUNG 1 number + verdict YES
segs.text: The pressure is now a hundred times what you're used to, like a heavyweight boxer standing on every fingertip of your skin. Alive? Yes. You just can't see a thing.

segs.label: RUNG 2 (1-2 km) creature: giant squid (teaser 1 paid)
segs.text: Just below the line, something huge drifts up beside you: a giant squid, up to the length of a bus, with an eye wider than your face, and it has turned toward you.

segs.label: RUNG 2 weapon + callback (dinner fights back)
segs.text: Its suckers are ringed with tiny teeth, and dead sperm whales wash up with those rings printed on their skin, like rows of bottle caps. Dinner fights back.

segs.label: RUNG 2 threat: nerves + honest unknown
segs.text: Then your hands start to shake, because at pressures like this nerves misfire: fingers tremble, rooms spin, people nod off mid-sentence. And at twice the record? Nobody knows. Nobody has been there.

segs.label: RUNG 2 verdict "?" (no cheat for a maybe)
segs.text: So your meter can't say yes or no. It says this. And a maybe doesn't earn a cheat, so you keep sinking, shaking, past two kilometres.

segs.label: RUNG 3 (2-3 km) threat: the cold
segs.text: And here's the problem nobody warned you about: the cold. The surface was as warm as a heated pool, and down here it's barely above freezing.

segs.label: RUNG 3 you-scenario + host ruling
segs.text: In water that cold, most people black out within half an hour, and you've been in it for over half an hour. Near three kilometres, you stop shivering. I'll be honest, this is where I'd have quit.

segs.label: DEATH 1 (33%)
segs.text: Alive? No. First death, fifty minutes in.

segs.label: Cheat 1
segs.text: Cheat number one: a heated suit. You wake up warm, still sinking, and you're not alone.

segs.label: RUNG 3 creature: beaked whale (at your depth)
segs.text: A slim grey whale with a short beak glides past you: a Cuvier's beaked whale, the deepest-diving mammal ever tracked, and one was followed almost exactly to your depth.

segs.label: RUNG 3 comparison (teaser 2 paid)
segs.text: It breathes air, just like you, and with no cheats at all, its longest breath on record lasted longer than your entire fall to the bottom.

segs.label: RUNG 4 (3-4 km) expectation reversal
segs.text: Nearly four kilometres down, you pass the average depth of the ocean, where most of the planet's seafloor would be.

segs.label: RUNG 4 geometry: onto the trench wall
segs.text: But you're over a trench, so the current nudges your sled against its wall, and you slide down it the rest of the way, with seven kilometres to go.

segs.label: RUNG 5 (4-5 km) ABYSS named, shells dissolve
segs.text: Four kilometres: the abyss. The water here is so cold and squeezed that seashells landing this deep slowly dissolve.

segs.label: Turnstile 1 (good news / bad news)
segs.text: Good news: you're not a seashell. Bad news: down here, you're food.

segs.label: RUNG 5 gross-out: bait cam
segs.text: When scientists drop a dead fish on slopes like this, long-tailed fish called grenadiers find it within half an hour, tiny scavengers swarm in, and within a day it can be bones.

segs.label: RUNG 5 threat on you + strategy + verdict
segs.text: And now the grenadiers are circling you. Strategy: keep moving, because if you nap down here, you become the event of the year. Alive? Yes. Being watched? Also yes.

segs.label: "Picture it again" re-immersion (47%)
segs.text: Picture where you are. Look up: the boat and the sunshine are over an hour of climbing above you. Look down: there's more water below you than above you.

segs.label: RUNG 6 (5-6 km) number
segs.text: Five kilometres. Every fingertip of your skin is now holding up a grand piano. Please don't try to play it.

segs.label: RUNG 6 creature: dumbo octopus
segs.text: Out of the dark flaps a dumbo octopus, waving two fins like cartoon elephant ears. It's about as long as your forearm and hand, and it lives deeper than any other octopus we know.

segs.label: Verdict MOSTLY + turnstile 2 (52%)
segs.text: Alive? Mostly. But that wall you're sliding along is about to become the problem.

segs.label: RUNG 7 (6-7 km) HADAL named
segs.text: Six kilometres. You've crossed into the hadal zone, the trenches, which cover a sliver of the seafloor but span almost half of the ocean's full depth.

segs.label: RUNG 7 mechanism
segs.text: Trenches form where one plate of Earth's crust dives under another, so they shake, and their walls collapse in avalanches of mud.

segs.label: RUNG 7 dated aside + strategy punished
segs.text: After the great Japan earthquake of twenty eleven, mud slid down the Japan Trench all the way to its floor. And your strategy was to keep moving along the wall, which is exactly where avalanches run.

segs.label: DEATH 2 (58%, sawtooth crash)
segs.text: The slope above you shudders, and a cloud of mud rolls over your sled. Alive? No. Second death.

segs.label: Cheat 2 + host ruling
segs.text: Cheat number two: the mud lets you go. You shake yourself off, still sinking, with a single cheat left. I did warn you about the wall.

segs.label: RUNG 8 (7-8 km) number
segs.text: Seven kilometres, and seven hundred times surface pressure, so every fingertip of your skin now has a dairy cow standing on it.

segs.label: RUNG 8 threat: molecules, verdict BARELY
segs.text: Now the pressure goes after your molecules. Proteins, the tiny machines your cells run on, get squashed out of shape, your cell membranes stiffen, and the chemistry of being alive starts to jam. Alive? Barely.

segs.label: RUNG 9 (8-9 km) SPOKEN FLIP (65%) + creature: snailfish
segs.text: Eight kilometres, and the question changes: not what kills you, but what can live where you can't. A snailfish, pink and see-through, like wet tissue paper with eyes, swims right up to your face.

segs.label: RUNG 9 mechanism + its ceiling
segs.text: Its body is packed with a molecule called TMAO that holds its proteins in shape. But the deeper a fish lives, the more it needs, and a little past eight kilometres, it would need so much that water would flood its body.

segs.label: Teaser 3 paid: the last fish
segs.text: The deepest fish ever filmed was a young snailfish just past that line. You just met the last fish on the planet.

segs.label: DEATH 3: the planted squeeze wins where the fish's TMAO runs out
segs.text: It turns back. You don't. The squeeze that was jamming your proteins keeps climbing, and right where even the fish's TMAO runs out, it wins. Alive? No. Third death.

segs.label: Cheat 3 (last), trick named + joke
segs.text: Cheat number three, your last: you borrow the trick of the tiny crustaceans down here, proteins built to hold their shape under the squeeze. You wake up slightly shrimpier, with no cheats left.

segs.label: STAKES RESET (end game starts)
segs.text: Die again, and the trip is over.

segs.label: Biggest landmark: one Everest down
segs.text: By now, you've sunk the full height of Mount Everest, and there are still two kilometres of water underneath you.

segs.label: OPTIONS 1/3: float up (killed by DEATH 2's wall)
segs.text: Can you save yourself? Drop the weights and float up? That's three more hours back along the wall that buried you once.

segs.label: OPTIONS 2/3: wait for rescue (killed by the sperm whale's depth)
segs.text: Wait for rescue? The deepest rescue in history happened shallower than where you heard that sperm whale. Nobody is coming.

segs.label: OPTIONS 3/3: hold your breath (killed by the squeeze) + joke
segs.text: Hold your breath like the beaked whale? Great plan, if you were a whale. Breath was never the problem. The squeeze is.

segs.label: RUNG 10 (9-10 km) creature + plant
segs.text: Nine kilometres. A tiny amphipod, about as long as the top joint of your thumb, chews on a sunken branch. Its gut turns wood into sugar, so whatever sinks ends up inside it. Remember that.

segs.label: Verdict YES, 0 cheats
segs.text: Alive? Yes. Cheats left? None. Lonely? Extremely.

segs.label: RUNG 11 (10-10.9 km) + arrival: Challenger Deep, three hours
segs.text: Ten kilometres, and then the sled thumps into soft mud. This is the bottom, Challenger Deep, the lowest point in the ocean, three hours after you left the boat.

segs.label: ZERO-CHEAT TEST: the squeeze peaks; the borrowed trick holds
segs.text: Every fingertip now carries more than a tonne, about a small car, and the squeeze that killed you is a third stronger. The needle slides toward no, and stops: the crustacean trick holds. Alive? Yes.

segs.label: Finished board + peak declared (88%)
segs.text: Final reading. Deaths: three. Cheats left: none. You beat the ocean, and honestly, it doesn't get any better than this.

segs.label: TWIST (89%): rule 3 turned around
segs.text: [pause: 0.5] Except you weren't the first thing of ours to get here without a submarine.

segs.label: Teaser 4 paid: the bag (reveal)
segs.text: In nineteen ninety-eight, a robot sub filmed it on the floor of this trench, almost at the bottom: a single-use plastic bag.

segs.label: Punch: rule 3 broken
segs.text: It beat you here. No cheats. No help.

segs.label: Callback to the plant: fibres (reveal)
segs.text: And the amphipod you met, the one that eats whatever sinks? Every one they opened had swallowed tiny fibres, and the ones they tested included plastic.

segs.label: Punch: the speck pays
segs.text: That grey speck in its gut? Ours.

segs.label: Escalation: PCBs (comparison on screen only)
segs.text: They also carried PCBs, industrial poisons banned decades ago, eleven kilometres from the nearest factory.

segs.label: Villain swap
segs.text: The cold, the mud, the fish's ceiling: not one of the things that killed you got there first. The newest arrival at the bottom of the world is ours.

segs.label: BOOKEND (mirror of frame 1) + left-open ending
segs.text: Picture the start again: calm water, sunshine, the boat. Your sled took three hours. Whatever slips into that water today starts the same trip, and nobody knows how long it takes. It just keeps arriving.
